title: Meshtastic: text messages with no cell service
summary: What Meshtastic is, how to choose radios, what region and preset to use, private channels, hop limit, battery notes, and why Richmond's MeshCore effort will not help.

blocks.text: **Meshtastic** lets phones send text messages with **no cell service and no Wi-Fi.** Small low-power radios pass messages to each other, and your phone talks to your own radio over Bluetooth. It is free to use, but **it has to be set up before the outage.**
What it is

items: The radios use **LoRa**, a low-power, long-range radio technology. The Meshtastic docs say it can reach "several kilometers" without cell, Wi-Fi or other infrastructure.
It is a **mesh**: radios repeat the messages they hear, so a message can hop across several radios to reach someone far away. No special router is needed.
A radio pairs with one phone at a time over Bluetooth. Each radio supports only one user connection at a time. Messages are encrypted.
Range: the docs give no typical range. The current record is 331 km (205 miles), which took special equipment and ideal conditions. **Test your own radios; do not count on a number.**

blocks.text: Never power on a Meshtastic radio without its antenna attached. The docs say it could damage the radio chip.
It must be set up beforehand

Flashing the radio's software, installing the app and creating your private channel all need a computer or phone and an internet connection. Do all of it now, then test. See the guide on setting up two Meshtastic radios.
Choosing a device
Meshtastic's docs group devices by manufacturer and chip. All listed boards can mesh with each other, so pick for your needs.

rows: Uses less power. The docs generally prefer it for solar and handheld use.
Uses more power but is usually cheaper. Does well on house power, suits a handheld that only needs a day or two of runtime, and supports Wi-Fi.

items: The docs strongly recommend radios with Semtech SX126x or LR11xx chips over the older SX127x.

Makers listed include RAK, LILYGO, Heltec, Seeed Studio, B&Q Consulting, Elecrow, M5Stack and Raspberry Pi. Community favorites named include the RAK4631 starter kit, the Seeed Card Tracker T1000-E, Heltec Mesh Node T114 and LILYGO T3-S3.
Buy at least two, and a USB cable that carries data, not only power. A quick test is to copy a file to or from a phone.

blocks.text: Region and preset

items: **Region: US.** This sets the legal frequency range, 902.0 to 928.0 MHz. Until a region is set, the radio does not transmit.
**Preset: LongFast.** A preset sets bandwidth, spreading factor and coding rate together. Radios on different presets cannot hear each other at any distance. LongFast is the default.
**Watch out:** a US radio whose region was first set from its own screen can start on LongTurbo, which cannot hear LongFast. Check the preset on every radio.

blocks.text: A higher data rate gives shorter range; a lower data rate gives longer range but takes longer to send.
The public channel and your private channel

items: Every radio has a **primary channel** (channel 0). On the default LongFast channel the key is publicly known, so **anyone can read what you send** there.
A **PSK** (pre-shared key) is the secret that encrypts a channel. Radios must share the same channel name and PSK to talk. A key is 16 or 32 bytes.

**For family privacy, make a separate private channel with your own random key** and keep the primary channel at its default. The docs advise adding private groups as secondary channels 1 to 7. They share your radio settings, and renaming the primary channel can move the radio to a different frequency.
A radio holds up to 8 channels (0 to 7), and active channels must be consecutive.
Direct messages to one person are encrypted to that person's key.

blocks.text: Sharing the channel by QR code

Your app shows a link or QR code for a channel. The other phone scans it, and that copies the channel name, key and radio settings. Only scan codes from someone you trust: scanning applies every setting in the code.
Hop limit

A **hop** is one relay. Every time a radio passes a message along, the message's hop limit drops by one, and at zero the next radio does not repeat it. The default hop limit is 3 and the maximum is 7. The docs say to keep the default.

blocks.alt: Diagram of a Meshtastic message. A phone connects by Bluetooth to your radio. Your radio sends by LoRa to a relay radio, which sends it to the family member's radio, which connects by Bluetooth to their phone. Each relay lowers the hop limit by one. The default hop limit is 3 and the maximum is 7.
blocks.caption: A message hops from radio to radio. The default hop limit is 3.

blocks.text: Battery and power

items: The docs recommend the **CLIENT** role for most people. The ROUTER role uses a lot of power.
The screen turns off after a timeout that defaults to 10 minutes. A shorter timeout saves power.
Power saving can turn off Bluetooth, serial, Wi-Fi and the screen. It suits solar setups, but it makes the radio harder to reach, so read the warnings first.
Leave transmit power at its default. The docs advise it for most people.

blocks.text: Local context: Richmond
**The VAMesh effort in the Richmond area uses MeshCore, which cannot talk to Meshtastic.** Radios from one will not hear the other.

Meshtastic's own local-groups list shows no Meshtastic community in the Richmond area that we could verify. **Plan on your own private channel with your own radios**, not on a public mesh being there when you need it.
Is it legal?

In most regions LoRa needs no extra license, unlike ham radio. In the US it uses the 902-928 MHz band under FCC Part 15. Do not choose the "ITU" amateur regions in the app without a ham license; the docs say those regions need licensed mode, no encryption, and your call sign on the air.
